## Review action items from previous meeting

### How to handle security notifications ([discussion #331](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/tsc/discussions/331))

Ry Jones (Linux Foundation) has set up a notification process and opened [security-tracking PR #119](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/security-tracking/pull/119), which adds a `notify.yaml` file and a manual workflow for adding collaborators to an advisory. Anyone with access to the security-tracking repository will be able to add a registered person to a specific security advisory, so that whoever is responsible for the affected algorithm implementation can see the advisory and receive notifications about it.

For now the process is manual: when an advisory concerning an algorithm comes in, someone has to add that algorithm's contact to the advisory by hand. A later version could map advisory labels or names to the responsible people and notify them automatically, but Rodrigo considers this a good starting point. He has reviewed the PR and it matches what the TSC asked for. Ry has asked for a second reviewer, and since Douglas owns the security-tracking repository, Rodrigo asked him to take a look. There were no comments.

## OpenSSL Conference reporting

Rodrigo, Michael, Norm and Bruce attended the OpenSSL Conference in Prague last week.

### Rodrigo

Rodrigo's goal was to show that OQS's mission continues: what has changed is which algorithms it covers, not what it does. He felt his talk was "a bit of a bust". Attendance was low and he got less audience interaction than he had hoped; next time he plans to offer small incentives, such as candy, for answering questions. All four OQS attendees had useful conversations, but he did not think this was the most productive conference for spreading the OQS message. Another theme all four noticed was how much AI has changed things for open source security projects over the past year. They also heard about progress on OpenSSL work and potential collaborations.

At least three people asked Rodrigo what the next step for OQS is, which he took as a good sign. Michael added that people clearly want OQS to keep including experimental algorithms. Rodrigo said people had also asked specifically about Falcon and HQC.

### Bruce

- **AI and security reports.** AI was a major topic, and Bruce saw two points of broad agreement. The first is that AI has made it easy for people with no expertise in secure coding or cryptography to file large numbers of security advisories. liboqs is seeing this too, and Bruce has struggled to keep up in recent weeks. Many reporters, probably using similar models, report the same vulnerability over and over in slightly different words. Because disclosure is private, they cannot see each other's reports, which creates a lot of overhead for maintainers. Bruce has started using AI to find duplicates, but that is not yet a reliable method. The second point is that maintainers everywhere are trying to use AI to automate their own workflows and cut the time spent handling the extra volume and noise, some with more success than others. One talk near the end, by an OpenSSL maintainer, described rude emails from reporters demanding attention ("my agent says this is super serious"; "how dare you say it's out of your threat model").
- **Bouncy Castle.** Bruce did not attend the Bouncy Castle talk (see Michael's report below), but noted that Bouncy Castle has integrated FAEST, QR-UOV and others into its Java library even though the reference implementations are all in C ([source](https://github.com/bcgit/bc-java/tree/main/core/src/main/java/org/bouncycastle/pqc/crypto)).
- **Red Hat.** Engineers from Red Hat are interested in continuing to ship liboqs and oqs-provider. The original reason, in 2024, was to give Red Hat Enterprise Linux customers easy access to ML-KEM and ML-DSA in OpenSSL for experimentation. Now Falcon and HQC are close to standardization, and customers want an easy way to experiment with those.
- **OpenSSH fork.** Some Cisco partners would like continued support for OQS's fork of OpenSSH. OpenSSH is selective about which algorithms it includes, and some Cisco customers want an experimental fork for trying non-standardized algorithms.

### Michael

- **OpenSSL and AI-generated security reports.** Tomáš Mráz's talk on how OpenSSL handles AI-generated security reports raised one observation that Michael found interesting: if two different people report the same issue, can it really still be under embargo? Does it have to go through the full GHSA/CVE process, or could it simply be fixed in the open as a normal issue? OpenSSL is a production library with much stricter requirements than OQS, an experimental one, yet even OpenSSL is considering this to cope with the volume. Nearly all of the AI-generated reports OpenSSL has received have been rated low severity. There was some internal debate over whether the official rating should be higher than OpenSSL's own, but in practice none has reached high or critical. The core problem is asymmetry: a reporter can have an LLM produce a write-up and test cases with very little effort, while maintainers have to take every report seriously. OQS is in a somewhat better position, since no one should rely on it in production. Michael saw this as vindication of his practice in oqs-provider of asking reporters to open a public PR. Reporters have agreed every time, and those issues were closed without going through the CVE/GHSA process. Hart noted in the chat that the [Linux kernel now treats security bugs found by publicly available LLMs as public](https://docs.kernel.org/process/security-bugs.html), on the assumption that others will find them too, and shared a [related news item](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/10/14/linux-kernel-devs-drop-obligatory-confession-of-ai-tool-usage/5303140).
- **Bouncy Castle.** Michael has known the Bouncy Castle team since about 2022, from an IETF hackathon. At the time it was the only other library with all of the PQ candidates, and it has kept that up. At this conference they described for the first time how they handled the latest round of signature algorithms: this time with AI, essentially done by one person. Michael found the approach sensible. They started with a single algorithm to learn how to do it, wrote skills to automate the following integrations, and added tooling, including constant-time checking, to port the reference implementations to Java and pass all the test vectors. Bouncy Castle has two providers: the default provider, which now includes ML-KEM and ML-DSA, and a separate PQ provider for all the experimental algorithms. Michael would like OQS to reach the same coverage soon so the two can be compared, for example at an IETF hackathon.
- **Red Hat.** Michael's conversations with Red Hat confirmed what Bruce heard: they are long-time oqs-provider users and still want it for experimental algorithms. He also asked whether removing the standardized algorithms from oqs-provider would cause them problems. They said it would be absolutely fine, since OpenSSL now provides those by default.
- **AI in security libraries.** Michael had expected his talk on building a provider with AI help to meet resistance or ridicule, but it was well received, and several OpenSSL committers were in the room. In his view AI is here to stay and will be accepted in security libraries such as OpenSSL too.

Douglas thanked everyone for giving presentations and talking to people at the conference.

## Classic McEliece future status

Rodrigo summarized the situation. For the past three or four months there have been reports of new cryptanalysis of Classic McEliece. About three weeks ago, the German BSI, one of Europe's strongest supporters of Classic McEliece, recommended not using it in future products. It did not deprecate existing deployments, but it advised against including Classic McEliece in new plans. liboqs does not have the ISO version of Classic McEliece, only the version from the NIST standardization process.

**Proposal.** Rodrigo proposed the approach that Bruce, Michael, Norm and he had discussed the previous week, modeled on what OQS did with HQC:

- In **liboqs 0.17**, keep Classic McEliece but disable it by default, with a disclaimer pointing to the recent cryptanalysis.
- In **liboqs 0.18**, remove it entirely.

Douglas said this largely makes sense. He and Bruce had discussed two factors that morning:

- **Doubts about the algorithm.** These come both from BSI and from the cryptanalysis. The impact of the cryptanalysis is not settled and is still being debated: the new results are distinguishers, while Classic McEliece's security generally rests on the one-wayness of the underlying problem, and the community has not reached consensus. BSI's statement, however, is something OQS can act on.
- **Unmaintained upstream.** The upstream implementation OQS uses is no longer maintained.

Together, these argue for working towards deprecation unless something substantial changes on both fronts. The proposal signals this clearly. There is no urgency to remove the algorithm in the next release, because it is not considered broken; if it were, the algorithm deprecation policy would require removing it. If someone in the community volunteers to maintain it and makes a strong case for keeping it, the TSC would revisit the decision, but that would have to come from the community.

Rodrigo added that the two-step approach leaves room to react to new developments. 0.17 will be a short release before the end of the year, and 0.18 will be a longer one following the normal process. If the cryptanalysis turns out to be less serious than it now appears, the plan can change.

**Rosenpass.** Logan explained that Rosenpass relies on Classic McEliece from liboqs, the pre-ISO version. Since there is no outright break, Rosenpass is not planning to change. He asked whether OQS would accept someone volunteering to maintain Classic McEliece and update it to the libmceliece version. Rodrigo gave his personal view. He assumes libmceliece follows the ISO version, which is not compatible with the pre-ISO one, so users face a migration either way. Anyone relying on the liboqs implementation has 0.16, where it is enabled by default, and 0.17, where it can be enabled alongside all the round 3 algorithms. He considers that sufficient support. Maintaining an algorithm that is no longer recommended and uses a lot of CI time does not make much sense to him given OQS's mission as a PQ research platform, even though the algorithm has not been shown to be broken. Michael asked Logan whether Rosenpass uses the liboqs version; Logan confirmed it does, so Rosenpass can work with the proposal or pin an older liboqs release. Logan also asked what would happen if the Classic McEliece team changed parameters to increase the security margin. Rodrigo said that would be a different algorithm and a separate discussion, and that he is not aware of any such plans.

There were no objections to the proposal.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** Add to the [liboqs 0.17.0 milestone](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/milestone/31): disable Classic McEliece by default, with a disclaimer pointing to the recent cryptanalysis and the BSI recommendation. Plan for removal in 0.18 unless the situation changes.

## OQS Provider discussion

Rodrigo noted that this item covers three related but distinct topics: dropping the standardized algorithms ([oqs-provider issue #821](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/821)), the separate [hybrid provider](https://github.com/baentsch/hybrid-provider) Michael presented in Prague, and a practical proposal for getting there ([oqs-provider PR #846](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/846)).

### Dropping standardized algorithms ([issue #821](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/821))

Today, oqs-provider checks the OpenSSL version at runtime and does not offer the standardized algorithms if OpenSSL supports them natively. The proposal is to stop offering standardized algorithms through the provider under any OpenSSL version. Earlier provider releases would still offer them. Following the same approach as for Classic McEliece in liboqs, the short oqs-provider 0.13 release that will accompany liboqs 0.17 could be announced as the last one to support the standardized algorithms, with support dropped in the following release.

Michael is fully in favor: it would make maintenance much easier. Yesterday he opened two PRs following the previous week's discussion:

- [oqs-provider PR #845](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/845) adds advisory code-complexity checks to CI (cyclomatic and cognitive complexity), to show concretely why simplifying the code helps. He asked for someone to review it so it can be merged and improvements tracked.
- [oqs-provider PR #846](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/846) is a draft/demo that removes the hybrid logic from oqs-provider, leaving a pure liboqs–OpenSSL bridge.

He also has an older feature branch, started when he began thinking about issue #821, that is well advanced in removing the standardized algorithms. The complexity measures show it simplifies the code considerably.

Rodrigo said the one argument he sees for keeping the standardized algorithms is that the provider gives access to liboqs's implementations of them, which differ from OpenSSL's, so the two can be compared. That can also be done with an earlier provider release, however, and supporting them generates a backlog of issues for functionality OpenSSL already provides. Michael added that, as an extreme AI experiment, he had built an mldsa-native provider without looking at the code at all, and it appears to work. Bouncy Castle's approach is essentially the same: take a low-level library and plug it in. People who want to try other implementations within OpenSSL can therefore do so easily. Rodrigo said the same argument could be made about almost anything. Michael agreed, and said this leads into a longer, separate discussion about whether OQS should keep its `copy_from_upstream` mechanism, since AI may now enable better ways of doing things. He suggested leaving that for another day.

No decision was taken on dropping the standardized algorithms.

### Separating out the hybrid logic

Rodrigo described oqs-provider as currently doing two different jobs. It is a wrapper between liboqs and OpenSSL (the provider proper), and it also implements the logic for hybrid algorithms in OpenSSL. In last week's discussion there was general agreement that separating the two would be an architectural improvement. One provider would bring liboqs's experimental (non-standardized) algorithms into OpenSSL. A separate hybrid provider would handle hybrids; this is still post-quantum research, so in Rodrigo's view it still belongs under OQS.

Douglas noted that both of Michael's experiments were AI-driven: removing the hybrid logic from oqs-provider (PR #846) and building the hybrid provider in his own repository. He asked whether Michael had also tried an AI-driven cleanup of the existing provider that keeps both functions. That would show whether the maintenance and technical-debt concerns come from having two things in one provider, or from how the code has grown over the years. Michael said he had not, and that his concern is the structure itself. AI does make mistakes, so asking it for a clean all-in-one provider would still be real work and is less attractive than the basic premise of splitting the functions. oqs-provider does many things, not just two or three. Besides PQ signatures and KEMs, it provides several kinds of hybrids: OpenSSL alone has at least two ways of combining algorithms, some standardized and some not, some at the TLS level and some not. In his view oqs-provider does far too much, however it is written.

Douglas also wants to understand how users actually use the provider. In the discussion on issue #821, Norm argued for the convenience of a single provider. Norm (at Cisco) is the only oqs-provider user Douglas knows of directly, although there are surely others, and Michael has talked to Red Hat. Douglas would like OQS to gather users' views more systematically on what a split would mean for them. Michael agreed and suggested announcing the plan and seeing who responds. Norm raised concerns in last week's discussion, but also said he is the one at Cisco who would rearrange the providers to make a split work. That is technically possible, with some extra scripting, and Cisco already ships two providers together (the default or FIPS provider plus oqs-provider). Douglas recalled that when the standardized algorithms first became available in both OpenSSL and oqs-provider, combining them was supposed to work but ran into problems, so this should be double-checked. Michael noted that the hybrid provider is genuinely new: it is a meta-provider that loads other providers, sitting both above and below OpenSSL. It seems to work, and his talk in Prague was well received.

In the chat, Dean mentioned that he has been using OQS to build reverse proxies that upgrade or downgrade the cryptographic protocol according to what the incoming traffic supports, and that the hybrid approach has worked well for him.

Rodrigo will collect feedback from oqs-provider users, such as Cisco (Norm has already given his view) and Red Hat, on whether they would use a hybrid provider and whether they would want one provider or two. Michael will open a separate issue for the hybrid provider discussion, since it got mixed into issue #821, which is only about the standardized algorithms. The TSC will come back to this at the next meeting once there is more feedback.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Michael):** Open a separate oqs-provider issue for discussing splitting out the hybrid logic and the hybrid provider.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** Contact oqs-provider users (such as Cisco and Red Hat) about whether they would use a separate hybrid provider and whether they want one provider or two, and collect the answers on that issue.
